e.etymology: From the Irish surname Callen, a variant of Callan. It took off as a first name after NCIS: Los Angeles introduced agent G. Callen in 2009.
namesakes: G. Callen (Chris O'Donnell's agent on NCIS: Los Angeles)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that pairs the Ky- of Kyle with the -son ending of Tyson and Bryson.
The medieval English form of French Louis, from Frankish Hludwig, famous in battle. It also served as an English stand-in for Welsh Llywelyn.
namesakes: Lewis Carroll (author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland)

assoc.t: Lewis and Clark expedition across the American West

e.etymology: The English form of German Friedrich, from Germanic words for peace and ruler. It stayed in the US top 100 from 1880 into the 1950s.
namesakes: Frederick the Great (18th-century king of Prussia)

assoc.t: Frederick Douglass, abolitionist and orator
Frederick, Maryland, city northwest of Washington, DC

e.etymology: A modern American name with no settled derivation, a longer spelling of Amiya in the same family of sounds as Amaya, Aaliyah and Mariah.
A medieval Norman French pet form of Alis (Alice), from Old High German Adalhaid, of noble kind. Chaucer used it as Alisoun in The Canterbury Tales.

assoc.t: Alison, Elvis Costello's 1977 song

e.etymology: A Spanish name, probably from the Guanche language of the Canary Islands and related to Guacimara. A less likely theory ties it to Guiomar, from Germanic Wigmar, battle famous.
e.note: The X is said like S (or Z), never ks; expect to coach people on spelling and pronunciation.

e.etymology: From an English surname meaning son of Ben, a short form of Benedict. In some families the surname comes instead from Benson, a village in Oxfordshire.
namesakes: Benson DuBois (Robert Guillaume's butler on Soap and Benson)

assoc.t: Olivia Benson of Law & Order: SVU
Benson, 1980s sitcom starring Robert Guillaume

e.etymology: A K spelling of Catalina, the Spanish form of Katherine. Katherine goes back to Greek Aikaterine, whose root is uncertain but was long linked to katharos, pure.

assoc.t: Catalina Island off Southern California (spelled with C)

e.etymology: A spelling of Emily common among Spanish-speaking families and also found in Germany. Emily comes from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to Latin aemulus, rival.
A medieval pet form of Robert, from Germanic words for fame and bright, that reached England through Old French. As a girls' name it is also taken from the red-breasted songbird.

assoc.t: Robin, Batman's sidekick
Robin Hood, outlaw of Sherwood Forest
robin, the red-breasted songbird

e.meaning: nourishing, kind; also soul in Spanish
e.etymology: Usually explained as Latin alma, nourishing or kind, as in alma mater; in Spanish alma is the word for soul. The name spread in English after the Battle of the Alma in 1854.

assoc.t: alma mater, the Latin phrase for one's old school

e.meaning: form of Luke, traditionally man from Lucania
e.etymology: A double-c spelling of Luca, the Italian form of Luke, from Latin Lucas and Greek Loukas. The spelling matches Lucca, the walled city in Tuscany.

assoc.t: Lucca, walled city in Tuscany, Italy

e.etymology: From the English surname Layne or Lane, given to a family who lived by a lane.
namesakes: Layne Staley (lead singer of Alice in Chains)

e.etymology: From the Scots word bonnie, fine or beautiful, likely from French bon, good. It began as an American nickname and is also a pet form of Bonita.
namesakes: Bonnie Parker (outlaw of Bonnie and Clyde)
Bonnie Tyler (singer, Total Eclipse of the Heart)

assoc.t: Bonnie Parker of the outlaw pair Bonnie and Clyde
Bonnie, the robot rabbit of Five Nights at Freddy's

e.etymology: From the color word scarlet, and a variant of Scarlett, an English surname for a dealer in scarlet cloth. Scarlett O'Hara of Gone with the Wind made the name famous.

assoc.t: Scarlet Witch, Marvel's Wanda Maximoff
The Scarlet Letter, Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel
Miss Scarlet, suspect in the board game Clue

e.etymology: A spelling of Casey, from the Irish surname Ó Cathasaigh, descendant of Cathasach, a byname meaning vigilant. It surged after Kayce Dutton appeared in the TV drama Yellowstone in 2018.
namesakes: Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes's character on Yellowstone)

assoc.t: Kayce Dutton, the youngest son on Yellowstone

e.note: Said KAY-see on Yellowstone, but the spelling also reads as KAYSS (like Jayce), so expect both.

e.etymology: From the name of the Franks, the Germanic people who gave France its name, and also a short form of Francis. It has stood as a formal given name since the 19th century.

assoc.t: frank, the word for candid and direct
Frank's RedHot cayenne pepper sauce
frank, short for frankfurter, a hot dog

e.etymology: The Scandinavian spelling of Eric, from Old Norse Eiríkr, read as ever ruler or sole ruler. Many kings of Denmark and Sweden bore it.
namesakes: Erik the Red (Viking who settled Greenland)

e.meaning: descendant of the dark brown one
e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Donndubháin, descendant of Donndubhán, a byname built from donn, brown, and dubh, black.
namesakes: Donovan (1960s folk-pop singer of Mellow Yellow)

assoc.t: Donovan, 1960s folk-pop singer of Mellow Yellow

e.etymology: A spelling of Colin, a medieval pet form of Col, itself short for Nicholas, Greek for victory of the people.
A modern American name in the style of Paisley and Hadley. It may also draw on the English surname and place name Hazley or Hazeley.
The Spanish form of Adam, written Adán in Spanish, from Hebrew adam, man, a word tied to earth and soil. In Genesis Adam is the first man.
The Hebrew form of Moses. Exodus explains it as drawn out, since the infant was pulled from the Nile; scholars also propose an Egyptian root meaning to give birth.
namesakes: Moshe Dayan (Israeli general and defense minister)

e.etymology: Coined for basketball player Jalen Rose, born in 1973, by blending the names of his father James and his uncle Leonard. His 1990s fame launched the name and spellings such as Jaylen.
From Ancient Greek Leonidas, son of Leon, built on leon, lion. Its most famous bearer is the Spartan king who died holding the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BC.
namesakes: Leonidas I (Spartan king who fell at Thermopylae)

assoc.t: King Leonidas of Sparta in the movie 300

e.etymology: From Latin and Greek lyra, lyre, the name of a small northern constellation. Philip Pullman's heroine Lyra in His Dark Materials brought it into wider use.
namesakes: Lyra Belacqua (heroine of Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials)

assoc.t: Lyra Belacqua, heroine of His Dark Materials
Lyra, constellation that holds the bright star Vega

e.etymology: From Hebrew Uri'el, God is my light, through Greek. In Jewish and Christian tradition Uriel is one of the archangels.
namesakes: Uriel (archangel in Jewish and Christian tradition)

e.etymology: From a surname, a variant of Kenrick with an added d. Kenrick is usually traced to the Old English name Cyneric, royal power, or to the Welsh name Cynwrig.

assoc.t: Kendrick Lamar, Pulitzer Prize-winning rapper

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname, from Old French portier, doorkeeper, or porteur, one who carries loads.

assoc.t: porter, a dark style of beer
porter, a baggage carrier at a hotel or station

e.etymology: A short form of Andrew, from Greek Andreas, built on the word for man, and sometimes of Andrea. Many American boys now receive it as their full name.
namesakes: Andy Griffith (actor, The Andy Griffith Show)

assoc.t: Andy, the boy who owns the toys in Toy Story
Raggedy Andy, rag doll brother of Raggedy Ann

e.etymology: An American nickname for a boy who is the third of his name, from triple, now given as a first name on its own. Tripp is also an English surname.

assoc.t: trip, the word for a stumble or a journey

e.note: Sounds exactly like the word trip, so jokes about stumbling are likely.
